articles.title: Karnataka drafts policy to monetise assets, eyes securities market
articles.summary: Bengaluru: Chief Minister D K Shivakumar’s office has drafted an asset monetisation policy to help the government raise funds by unlocking the value of its immovable properties, including through financial instruments floated in the securities market. The potential foray into the securities market via a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) will be a first for Karnataka. Fiscal pressures created by the flagship ‘guarantee’ schemes, coupled with ballooning revenue expenditure, has forced the government to look at asset monetisation to mobilise additional resources. The chief minister’s office has asked the Resource Mobilisation Committee (RMC), headed by retired bureaucrat K P Krishnan, to examine the draft policy. “If the government wants to mobilise additional resources through monetisation, then it is better to have a proper policy,” an official with direct knowledge of the matter told DH . “What is being proposed is an enabling environment,” the official added. Karnataka aims to emerge as global hub for AI, deep tech and semiconductor manufacturing: CM DK Shivakumar at Bengaluru Tech Summit According to sources in the RMC, several government-owned assets are being considered for monetisation. Apparently, assets belonging to the Karnataka Soaps & Detergents Ltd, the maker of the famous Mysore Sandal Soap, show promise through the REIT route. REIT is a financial instrument that allows investors to pool money to invest in income-generating properties. Such properties are placed under a trust that raises money by issuing units to investors through the securities market. Investors earn returns from the income generated by these properties, while the owner receives funds upfront without having to sell the assets. “REIT is definitely one of the modes of monetisation. The policy will keep all options open as permitted and choice of the instrument will depend on the specific circumstances and cases,” the official said.

articles.title: A village burned, its people killed or exiled
articles.summary: As his village burned, Mustafa Kamal somehow kept his family safe. Husband and wife, three sons, three daughters, a granddaughter, they ran until their breath ran out. They stumbled past bodies of people they knew, shot by Myanmar’s security forces. They slogged through mud that claimed some of their clothes and trekked over jungle passes thick with leeches. Days later, when they finally crossed a river into Bangladesh, they rowed past swollen bodies of other Rohingya Muslims who never made it to the other side alive. On Thursday, the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that the atrocities against the Rohingya ethnic minority constitute a genocide waged by the Myanmar State. The killing, gang rape and mass arson reached a furious zenith in 2017, building on years of systematic persecution. Three quarters of a million Rohingya flooded into Bangladesh in a matter of weeks, the most rapid refugee exodus in recent history. And more kept coming. A judgment in a country half a world away would matter, Kamal told me. It would acknowledge the fate of his home, Zammona, one of 400 Rohingya villages that were obliterated by Myanmar security forces nine years ago. But sitting in the dark, cramped shelter that is now his home in Bangladesh, part of what is now the world’s largest refugee settlement, Kamal said the trauma did not end nine years ago. For the Rohingya, he said, misery never ends. Muhammad Yunus' ancestral home set ablaze as violence grips Bangladesh International aid to the camps has plummeted. Hunger and disease are rampant. In May, Kamal’s 18-year-old son was killed by Rohingya militants who have unleashed a reign of terror in the refugee camps. Human traffickers roam the narrow spaces between tarpaulin shelters, grabbing men, women and children. One of Kamal’s daughters was kidnapped by a militant, who forced himself on her. She had no choice but to marry him, and they now have a baby boy. “Oh, Allah, why is there no justice for the Rohingya anywhere on earth?” Kamal said, weeping as he clutched a photo of his dead son. Kamal, now 66, grew up in Zammona, a fertile collection of hamlets in Myanmar’s far west, dotted with fish ponds, well-stocked groceries and mosques with graceful arches. His father was a teacher at a government school. Kamal learned Burmese, the language of Myanmar’s Buddhist Bamar majority, and took a job as a trader, ferrying goods from one town to another. His wife, Toyuba Khatun, was educated, too. The Rohingya had long faced repression from the military, which ruled Myanmar for decades and preserved power for the Bamar. In the 1980s, the Rohingya lost their legal status in Myanmar, their citizenship essentially stripped from them. Babies rarely were issued birth certificates. There was also occasional tension with the Rakhine ethnic group, with whom the Rohingya shared Rakhine state. Still, Kamal said he had easy relations with Rakhine villagers who lived nearby. After all, he had gone to school with them; his father had been their teacher. A store owner in Zammona, Mohammed Yunus said he welcomed Buddhist customers, bantering with them as they haggled over the latest clothes or electronics. (Zammona is called Zin Paing Nyar in the Burmese language.) In 2012, violence flared between the Rohingya and the Rakhine, inflamed by State media coverage. Gatherings of more than five Rohingya were banned. Mosques were shuttered. Many Rohingya children no longer felt welcome at government schools. Kamal’s father secretly taught his grandchildren at home, desperate for the next generation to be educated. When Kamal’s daughter Rehana Bibi got married, a Myanmar official forbade her from having more than two children. A false narrative took hold across Myanmar that the high birthrate of Rohingya was part of a global Muslim plot to swamp Buddhist lands. Military propaganda inaccurately portrayed the Rohingya as immigrants without legal status from Bangladesh. Never mind that Rohingya had been elected to parliament, studied at the nation’s finest universities, and once enjoyed government radio broadcasts in their own language, just like any other of the nation’s many ethnic groups. In the 2015 elections, which elevated the party of Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel Peace laureate, the Rohingya lost their right to vote. On October 9, 2016, a militant group led by a Rohingya refugee who was born in Pakistan and schooled in Saudi Arabia launched attacks on Myanmar security outposts, killing nine police officers, according to Myanmar authorities. The security forces’ response to the attacks punished an entire ethnicity. In Zammona, Kamal locked the door to his spacious wooden house and prayed with his family that the soldiers would not attack. Over the next few months, soldiers rounded up men in Zammona, accusing them of participating in the militant raids, charges they denied. Their only crime, they said, was being young, able-bodied Rohingya men. One was given a 54-year prison sentence. Soyadul Amin and Abdul Rohim were sentenced to 16 years each. Amin described how the Myanmar soldiers tied his arms behind his back, threw him on the ground and laughed as they ordered him to lap up his food like an animal. When he and others cried out for water, the soldiers offered urine. The United Nations said at the time that hundreds of Rohingya were killed and that the crackdown “very likely” constituted crimes against humanity. “We could not imagine what would happen next,” Kamal said. On August 25, 2017, the Rohingya militants carried out another series of attacks, killing more than a dozen security forces. This time, the military was prepared. Within hours, the scorched-earth retribution began. Kamal heard the rocket launchers crescendo from the east. He gathered his family, but there was no time to grab anything, apart from a few precious papers that proved their existence in Myanmar. As the soldiers descended on Zammona, Fatema Khatun, the wife of Amin, one of the men sent to prison, searched frantically for her seven children and thanked Allah that they were all there. She was seven months pregnant with her eighth child. Along their long escape to Bangladesh, a Myanmar soldier grabbed one of her daughters, Sukura Begum, in the forest and raped her, just one horror in what UN investigators say was systematised sexual violence. She was 11 years old. At least 10,000 Rohingya were killed by security forces and Rakhine mobs in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 attacks, the UN estimated. In Zammona, 10 unarmed men were trussed and killed, then tossed in a mass grave north of the village, said a Myanmar soldier whose testimony, after he ended up in the hands of an enemy militia, marked the first time perpetrators confessed to their crimes. The soldier also said seven Rohingya were shot dead there. Zammona was wiped from the map, its ruins smouldering for days, visible from a hill in Bangladesh. When he was released from a Myanmar prison four years later, his 16-year sentence commuted, Rohim returned home before he, too, fled across the border. In Bangladesh, Kamal and his family were allotted a tiny shelter with a tarpaulin cover. They could not leave the refugee camps without permission. International assistance allotted each person $12 a month for food, decreased now to $10. Fatema Khatun’s daughter, who was raped, suffers from debilitating seizures. Three years ago, another daughter, then 18, disappeared for months, then called tearfully from Malaysia, where she said she had been trafficked. She was forced to marry an older man, she said, 50 or 60 years old, she wasn’t sure.

articles.title: Congress has decimated idea of BJP: Rahul Gandhi
articles.summary: Washington: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has said that his party has decimated the idea of the BJP politically and the effect will be seen over the next eight months. Interacting with students at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, Gandhi claimed that the BJP’s internal structure has collapsed and the ministers in the government were in touch with the opposition, sharing information with them. "We have basically decimated the idea of the BJP politically in India today. It's done," Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, said in the interaction moderated by Professor Robert Pape. Gandhi said it took a group of disorganised students to shake up the BJP’s control over various arms of government. 'Indian democracy would end that very instant': Rahul Gandhi on why Opposition won't boycott elections "Please notice that organisation in India is fully in the hands of the BJP. The state police, the intelligence apparatus, the CBI, the IRS, the bureaucracy, everything in their control," he said. "Then, a couple thousand students come out onto the streets of Delhi, totally disorganised. And who won that contest? Do you think the police won the contest? No. The disorganised students won the contest,” Gandhi said. He described the Congress as a party of unorganised resistance, likening it to ‘Shivji ki Baraat’ – a big tent where people of all hues come together. "You've heard the term Shiv Ki Baraat? It's like that. It's disorganised, but has a central rhythm of organisation. It is the only way you can actually organise India because it's so complex,” Gandhi said, responding to a question on the splintered opposition in India. He said even when it was fighting the British, the Congress did not look like a military unit. “It has always been a party of unorganised resistance. It was unorganised, but inside the chaos, there were some rules of order,” he said. Gandhi said the Congress party had a very young leadership, who would soon find a place at the national level. He said the media tends to focus on a very small group of people within the Congress. “If you actually look at the Congress Party's structure, if you look at the people who are running our districts, if you look at the broad leadership of the Congress Party, they're very young. But they're not exposed to TV,” Gandhi said. “They're in the background. The real political fight occurs there. It doesn't actually occur in the TV studio. It occurs on the ground. And on the ground, I would say we are actually quite a young party,” Gandhi said. “We've been working on this over the last three, four, five, seven years. And we've got a very large number of very young, excellent people who are standing there. You'll start to see these people more and more at the national level. It is only a question of time,” Gandhi said.

articles.title: 3 lakh evacuated, 423 rescue teams deployed, 69 trains cancelled as cyclone 'Akvan' heads to Odisha
articles.summary: Bhubaneswar/Amaravati: Over 3 lakh people have been evacuated, and 423 rescue teams have been deployed in vulnerable areas of Odisha as the state stepped up its preparations ahead of the severe cyclonic storm 'Akvan', which is likely to make landfall between Puri and Gopalpur on Friday afternoon, officials said. The Odisha government has also set up 9,341 cyclone shelters across potentially affected districts as the storm—the third of its kind to threaten the state in 24 days—changed its trajectory over the past 24 hours after initially being projected to make landfall in Andhra Pradesh. Also on Thursday, the East Coast Railway cancelled 41 trains and rescheduled 29 others as a precautionary response to the cyclonic storm, an official said. The South Eastern Railway also cancelled at least 28 express trains, mostly going to or passing through the temple town of Puri on Friday. Cyclone 'Akvan': Odisha government evacuates over 1 lakh people, sets up 9,299 shelters Special Relief Commissioner (SRC) Rajesh P Patil said 2,98,676 people had been evacuated by Thursday evening and shifted to 2,523 relief camps. "Akvan is now moving towards Odisha at 13 kmph and is likely to cross the coast around Friday afternoon," an official of the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said. The official added that the storm lay around 410 km from Gopalpur and 470 km from Puri in Odisha on Thursday evening. Iran suggested the name 'Akvan' as part of the naming system for cyclones in the North Indian Ocean. IMD Director General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said 'Akvan' will cross the coast as a cyclonic storm, with wind speeds of 90-100 kmph. "The centre of the cyclone, known as the eye in meteorological terms, will cross the coast near Gopalpur in Odisha. Southern Andhra Pradesh will experience wind speeds of 90-100 kmph. In Odisha, wind speeds are expected to be 70-80 kmph," he said. Mohapatra said the system would gradually weaken while moving northwards through Odisha. "The projected path of Cyclone Akvan indicates that it is likely to cross the coast between Puri and Gopalpur around Friday noon," Chief Secretary Anu Garg said. Garg said that apart from deploying 60 teams of the Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF), 14 teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and 131 teams of the Fire and Emergency Services, the state government had requested the Indian Coast Guard to keep its helicopters, vessels and other logistics ready for relief and rescue operations. The chief secretary said arrangements were being made at the cyclone shelters to provide cooked and dry food to people and children, along with essential medicines, drinking water, sanitary napkins, and other necessary facilities. Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari said the government was also focusing on preventing landslides, which have emerged as a major challenge during cyclones. "We have identified as many as 941 locations vulnerable to landslides across five districts -- Ganjam, Gajapati, Kandhamal, Koraput and Malkangiri. The highest number of 211 such locations is in Gajapati district," the minister said. He added that 10 people had died in landslides during the previous cyclone, 'Arnab'. Cyclone Arnab kills three in Andhra Pradesh; over 87,000 evacuated across states, flights and trains cancelled Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi, who reviewed the state's preparedness, stressed the need to maintain the government's zero-casualty mission. As part of the precautions, tourists have been prohibited from visiting coastal areas, including Gopalpur, Puri, Satapada and Chilika, and fishermen have been asked not to venture into the sea, the chief secretary said. The coastal and southern regions of the state have been experiencing light to moderate rain since Wednesday night, and the intensity will increase gradually as the weather system nears the coast, Bhubaneswar Meteorological Centre Director Manorama Mohanty told reporters here. The state government has closed educational institutes in districts placed under 'red' (take action), 'orange' (be prepared) and 'yellow' (be aware) warnings, an official said, adding that rescue teams have been deployed in Malkangiri, Koraput, Rayagada, Kalahandi, Gajapati, Ganjam, Kandhamal, Boudh, Puri, Nayagarh and Khurda districts. The authorities of the Jagannath Temple in Puri urged devotees to plan their visits in accordance with weather advisories. The Gundicha Temple in Puri will remain closed to visitors from November 19 to 21. However, the 12th-century Jagannath Temple continues to remain open, with daily rituals being performed as usual, officials said. "We humbly request all devotees to plan their Shree Mandira darshan keeping in view the weather conditions arising from Severe Cyclonic Storm #Akvan and the official advisories. May Mahaprabhu Shree Jagannatha protect and bless us all!" Shree Jagannath Temple Administration (SJTA) Chief Administrator Arabinda Padhee said. The Nandankanan Zoological Park and the adjoining State Botanical Garden in Bhubaneswar will remain closed to visitors on November 19 and 20, officials said. The Bhitarkanika National Park in Kendrapara district has also been closed for three days till November 21 as a precautionary measure. The Similipal Tiger Reserve in Mayurbhanj district will also remain closed to visitors on November 20 and 21, they added. For Andhra Pradesh, the IMD has issued a red alert for Srikakulam and Vizianagaram districts, an orange alert for Parvatipuram Manyam, Alluri Sitaramaraju (ASR) and Anakapalli districts, and a yellow alert for Kakinada. A red alert indicates extremely heavy rainfall exceeding 20.44 cm in 24 hours, while an orange alert signifies very heavy rainfall of 11.56 cm to 20.44 cm and a yellow alert signifies heavy rainfall of 6.45 cm to 11.55 cm. The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) advised people in North Andhra to remain alert and urged farmers to take precautions while carrying out agricultural activities. Fishermen were advised not to venture into the sea.
